scenes.headline: How a model stores 128 experts and runs 8
scenes.sub: Routing, capacity and balance, then a real router read layer by layer
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Marshal. A mixture of experts keeps many feed-forward networks and runs a few per token. Who decides?

states.say: Qwen3 has a hundred and twenty-eight experts in each of its forty-eight layers.

states.term: Router: one matrix that scores every expert
states.say: For each token, a router picks eight of them. The rest sit idle for that token.

steps.say: The router scores every expert with one matrix and a softmax.
It keeps the eight highest. Every other expert gets a weight of zero.
The eight weights are rescaled so they add up to one.
The token's output is those eight experts' outputs, weighted and summed.
GShard put this layer inside the Transformer, in every other block, with two experts per token.

steps.term: All-to-all: every device sends to every other
steps.say: Spread over devices, each token travels to its experts and back. Two exchanges in every layer.

steps.label: Capacity factor 1.0
steps.term: Capacity: slots per expert per batch
steps.say: Hardware wants fixed shapes, so each expert gets a fixed number of slots. Busy experts overflow.

steps.label: Capacity factor 1.5
steps.say: Overflow tokens are dropped and ride the residual connection. More slots drop fewer, and empty slots still cost.

steps.label: Balanced routing, factor 1.0
steps.say: Even routing fits a small buffer. That is why every mixture of experts fights for balance.

steps.term: Bias: shifts who gets chosen, not the output
steps.say: Balance used to come from an extra loss that fights the main one. DeepSeek replaced it with a bias, used only to choose.
Overloaded experts get their bias lowered, idle ones raised. No gradient touched.
Where the balance is measured matters. Balanced per sequence, every domain spreads evenly.
Balanced over a whole batch, experts specialise. Code and maths find their own experts.

steps.caption: 32,768 tokens, 48 layers, every choice logged
steps.say: So I read a real router. Qwen3 on my 3090, every expert choice in all forty-eight layers, over code, prose, word problems and LaTeX.
Pooled over all four, the load is a smooth slope. Almost every expert gets used.

steps.caption: prose: 802 of 6,144 cells never chosen
steps.say: Split by domain, it breaks apart. Each domain leaves hundreds of experts untouched.

scenes.title: Experts a domain never touches, per layer
scenes.say: In an average layer, prose never reaches about seventeen of the hundred and twenty-eight experts. Code and prose share almost none of their busiest experts.

scenes.title: Experts one batch reads, per layer

steps.say: A batch reads the union of what its tokens chose. Eight users touch nearly forty-seven experts a layer, close to a random guess.
Consecutive tokens from one sequence share experts, so sixty-four of them read only half the layer.

scenes.label: of expert work dropped at capacity factor 1.0, one-sequence batches
scenes.note: measured; a factor near 15 would drop nothing
scenes.say: Put that routing through a Switch-style buffer and a single sequence's batch loses half its expert work. Specialised models run without a fixed buffer.

scenes.text: Balance over the corpus lets experts specialise by domain, and that is why modern MoE drops no tokens.
scenes.say: Balance over the whole corpus, and experts specialise. That is the trade every modern mixture of experts makes.

recap: Capacity drops overflow; balance decides how much
scenes.say: A router that picks a few, a buffer that drops the overflow, and experts that learn their domain. Thanks for watching!
